newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria institute sees 97 lev/dlr rate at 2-3,000.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria institute sees 97 lev/dlr rate at 2-3,000.

text.p: The lev/dollar exchange rate will average etween 2,000 and 3,000 this year depending on how early reform is launched, the Economy Institute at the Bulgarian Academy of Sciences said on Tuesday.

"Depending on the time of introduction of the currency board and the pre-board stabilisation measures, the rate will be between 2,000 and 3,000," the institute's deputy director Ivan Angelov told a news conference.

Bulgaria plans to introduce a fixed exchange rate regime under a currency board in June to restore confidence in its financial system as part of a $510 million accord signed with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) last month.

"It is possible to have the lev at 2,000 to the dollar if the currency board is introduced as early as June. But if it takes longer to introduce it, in August or September, there is risk of new depreciation," said Angelov.

The currency board system would require levs in circulation to be matched by central bank reserves, severely curbing the financial powers of the government and the central bank and preventing the printing of money.
Parliament will also have to decide to which currency to peg the lev, the dollar or the mark. IMF officials have said the exchange rate will be fixed at the market rate at the time.
The lev, after hitting a 3,000 per dollar record low in February from 600 at the beginning of January, has recovered to around 1,600 now.

Angelov urged the government to speed up economic reform to compensate for the delays of the past seven years and to pre-empt attempts to block it by opponents of reform in the state administration and some business groups.

He warned that corrupt business interests involved in asset stripping of state companies would attempt to discredit the currency board system and cause it to fail. He urged the government to act firmly against crime and corruption.
Angelov criticised some of the government's macroeconomic targets as unrealistic.
"To bring down monthly inflation to two percent at the end of the year from the three-digit levels in the beginning of the year, sounds more than optimistic," he said.

Cumulative inflation for the first two months of this year stood at 392 percent, February year-on-year inflation was 1,839 percent. The interim government expects March monthly inflation at around 12 percent.
Angelov also saw the low budget deficit of 3.8 percent of gross domestic product estimated by the IMF for this year as a difficult target after last year's 12 percent deficit.
"Few countries in Europe achieve a three percent budget deficit and to expect this from Bulgaria's crisis-ridden economy is too much," said Angelov.
The institute's projections are offered to the government and the central bank for reference in drafting economic policy.
